author: Declaration Desk
title: Qatari mediators float Hormuz-for-blockade trade as US sends third carrier toward Iran
dek: Regional officials told AP talks have advanced, but the US struck near Qeshm, Israel is reported to be lobbying for more strikes and Gulf states warn against them.
body:
Qatari mediators are trying to build a framework under which Iran would stop attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in return for the United States lifting its blockade of Iranian ports, according to two regional officials quoted by the Associated Press. The officials, who spoke anonymously about classified briefings they had received, said the mediators held two rounds of talks with Iranian officials last week and more are planned this week. Neither Washington nor Tehran has confirmed the framework, and the claim rests on those unnamed officials.

The diplomacy is running alongside military pressure. On Monday a US official told AP that American forces had carried out limited "defensive" strikes on some Iranian targets in the strait, after "Iranians using surface to air missiles against U.S. assets". Iranian state television reported explosions on Qeshm Island. AP said the strikes appeared limited, not a return to full hostilities, but they came after President Donald Trump had said the US would not launch new strikes on Iran before Tuesday's midterm elections.

## What happened

Vice President JD Vance, asked about a letter he sent last week to Iran's security chief Mohsen Rezaei, said on Monday: "We've had a number of good conversations with the Iranians. Look, the president and I both feel pretty good about the prospects for potentially coming to a negotiated settlement." Trump has said the letter was about helping Iran with "medical supplies and various things"; the White House has given few details. Vance also said: "We've certainly made some progress. We'll see if we can make some more," Agence France-Presse reported.

Rezaei told Iranian state television he had read the letter and had not replied, adding that "the tone has completely changed", which he called a "very good sign". He said Iran would keep blockading the strait until its conditions, including release of frozen assets, are met, according to Arab News. Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi told state media that "consultations and deliberations are very intensive", and that "Qatar and Pakistan are playing a very active mediating role". He described the plan on the table as a two-day sequence: on the first day, the US takes a set of measures; on the second, the strait reopens and traffic returns to normal.

## Background

The war began in late February. A ceasefire followed in the spring, and a June interim arrangement crumbled later in the summer, Arab News reported. The Strait of Hormuz, which carried about a fifth of the world's oil and a large share of liquefied natural gas before the crisis, has been the main front since. In September Iran proposed a seven-day plan to reopen it; its demands, as AFP summarised them, include ending the war on all fronts, unfreezing Iranian assets, lifting oil sanctions and ending the US counter-blockade of Iranian ports. AP reported that October saw the most attacks on commercial ships in the strait since March, and that the US and Israel have twice attacked Iran while it was negotiating over its nuclear programme, which is why Tehran wants guarantees that the US will implement its side of any deal.

AP said thousands of US troops remain off Iran to maintain the blockade and that a third aircraft carrier and thousands more troops are on their way to the Middle East. It put the cost of the war to US taxpayers at no less than $47 billion. Trump said in a speech on Monday: "I don't know if you even call it a war, because we haven't been doing any fighting for months."

## Reactions

Israel and its Gulf neighbours are pulling in different directions, AP reported. Two regional officials and a third person familiar with the matter said Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has pushed for another wave of strikes after the US election and is working with senior US officials to persuade Trump to launch a quick but extensive air campaign. One official said Trump does not appear to have decided. A person briefed on a weekend call said Trump would not commit. The Israeli government did not comment and the White House did not respond directly. AP's sources linked Netanyahu's push to his position after his bloc lost its parliamentary majority in last week's election; we have not independently confirmed that link.

Other US allies in the region are warning against new strikes, a third regional official told AP, arguing that they would destabilise the region and could lead Yemen's Houthis to step up attacks on Saudi Arabia and Red Sea shipping, and draw in Iran-backed militias in Iraq. At the Manama Dialogue security summit in Bahrain, UAE presidential adviser Anwar Gargash said the US and Iranian positions are far apart and "if these positions are not bridged, then we have to worry about the worst". Egypt's Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty said the next escalation "will be more dangerous, more destructive, and it will lead to nowhere".

On the Iranian side, Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei met military chiefs and said the response to "any kind and level of threat" from the US or Israel should be immediate and without "geographic limits", AP reported. First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref described the messages received from Washington as "an acknowledgement of our victory", according to AFP. Beyond the Gulf, China said it will send a special envoy to Iran, Oman and Saudi Arabia in early to mid-November, a foreign ministry spokesperson said, and AFP reported that Rezaei discussed the conflict with Russian President Vladimir Putin.

## Why it matters for India

India imports most of its crude oil and a large share of its gas, much of it from the Gulf, so the strait's status feeds directly into fuel prices, the rupee and inflation. Oil prices fell sharply on Monday on signs of progress; AFP put the fall at more than 7%, before the strike reports. Indian seafarers have been caught in attacks on shipping in the Gulf in recent days.

## What happens next

- More Qatari-mediated contacts are expected this week, according to AP's sources.
- The US midterms were held on Tuesday US time; the result will shape how much room Trump has.
- A Chinese envoy is due in the region in early to mid-November.
- Whether the reported framework becomes an agreement, or the US resumes large-scale strikes, is undecided on the evidence available.

## Key numbers

- 2: rounds of Qatari-Iranian talks last week (regional officials, via AP)
- 2 days: length of Iran's proposed reopening sequence (Araghchi)
- A third US aircraft carrier is on its way to the region (AP)
- $47 billion: minimum cost of the war to US taxpayers (AP)
